content: 1. Functional limitations in adults over 18 years of age are being considered for housing adaptations. These individuals often experience impairments in one or more areas of the Functional Independence Measure motor scale. For older adults, no minimum age is specified, but functional difficulties are self-reported in at least one activity of daily living (ADL) and at least two instrumental activities of daily living (IADL). 2. Adults aged 20 years and older, as well as all age groups, who are recipients of housing adaptations, often face problems in daily life and request home modifications. These modifications are typically related to areas such as entering and exiting the home, indoor mobility, and self-care in the bathroom. 3. Adults over 40 years of age may experience limitations in the type and amount of activities or work they can perform. They may also receive financial support or insurance due to disability, have sensory or communication limitations, or require mobility devices or prosthetics. 4. Frail older adults, defined by Fried frailty criteria (≥3), often lose functional autonomy as measured by functional autonomy systems. This group typically includes individuals aged 65 years and older. 5. Dementia-related interventions were not specifically provided, but adults with no minimum age specified were included in studies. 6. Home modifications to improve accessibility were implemented either as standalone interventions or as part of multi-component programs. These modifications often included architectural changes, such as grab bars, ramps, and widened doors, targeting mobility issues. Some interventions also focused on lighting improvements to address vision-related challenges. 7. A unique intervention involved installing a light path near the bed combined with tele-assistance to reduce nighttime falls among frail older adults. 8. One randomized controlled trial (RCT) used a factorial design to evaluate the effects of home safety programs, exercise programs, and social visits, both individually and in combination. 9. Cross-sectional studies reported associations between accessible home environments, improved ADL performance, and enhanced quality of life. 10. Accessibility features identified in studies included grab bars in bathrooms, ramps, wheelchair-accessible doors, automatic door openers, and improved lighting. These features targeted mobility, vision, and safety. 11. Home modifications were shown to reduce perceived difficulties in performing ADLs/IADLs, particularly in bathroom use and entry access. However, mobility and transfer difficulties did not significantly change in some cases. 12. Safety improvements, such as reduced falls and injuries, were observed following home modifications. For example, one RCT reported a 41% reduction in falls among older adults with severe visual impairments after a home safety program. 13. Multi-component interventions, including home modifications and training in problem-solving strategies, were associated with lower mortality rates up to two years post-intervention. 14. Quality of life improvements were noted in studies involving home modifications, particularly among individuals with physical impairments or low vision. However, no significant associations were found between quality of life and home safety features in adults with dementia. 15. Psychological benefits, such as reduced fear of falling and decreased feelings of depression, were reported following home accessibility interventions. These effects were particularly significant among older adults with functional difficulties. 16. Occupational performance, including self-care, productivity, and leisure activities, improved significantly after home modifications, especially among low-income adults with functional impairments. 17. Accessibility problems were significantly associated with reduced participation and autonomy, highlighting the importance of home modifications in promoting independence. 18. Overall, accessible home environments were found to improve health, well-being, and ADL/IADL performance among individuals with disabilities. Physical health benefits included reductions in falls and injuries, while psychological effects included less fear of accidents and improved mental health. 19. The systematic review emphasized the need for further research to guide the development of evidence-based guidelines for accessible home environments, particularly for individuals with functional impairments.
